Uzbekistan remains committed to the peaceful and responsible use of outer space and supports international efforts to keep space safe, secure and accessible for future generations. Thank you, Chair. Allow me on behalf of the delegation of Ecuador to congratulate you on your election to chair this period of sessions of the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. Likewise, we express our thanks to the Board, the Director of UNOSA, and to the Secretariat for the organization and management of our work this session. My delegation aligns itself with the statements made by the Group of 77 plus China and GRULAC. In a national capacity, we have the following comments. Mr. Chair, Ecuador reiterates its strong commitment to the use and exploration of outer space exclusively for peaceful purposes, to benefit all of humanity and in line with the principles of international law and the UN treaties on outer space. We consider that outer space constitutes a strategic area to promote sustainable development, strengthen international cooperation, and generate innovative solutions in the face of global challenges such as climate change, disaster risk management, food security, natural resource management, and the development of scientific and technological capacity. Thus, Ecuador recognizes the important role played by space applications in improving quality of life and contributing to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Satellite telecommunications, navigation, Earth observation and other space technologies are fundamental tools to support decision making based on well founded decisions and strengthen the resilience of our societies. Mr. Chair, Ecuador considers that access to outer space and the benefits that derive from its applications should be carried out in a way that is equitable, inclusive and non discriminatory. Developing countries must have real opportunities to participate actively in space activity. and they must benefit from the scientific and technological advances generated by the international community. Thus, we reiterate the importance of strengthening international cooperation mechanisms, knowledge transfer, exchange of experience and capacity development, such that space activities can continue being a tool to close gaps and promote sustainable development. Likewise, We recognize that there is a need to continue fostering initiatives that promote long-term sustainability of space activity, as well as responsible use of outer space, and strengthening of multilateral mechanisms in order to preserve outer space for present and future generations. Mr. Chair, my country attaches particular importance to the debates related to the future of space governance at the international level, and we are observing with great interest the preparations for UNISPACE IV. This process represents an opportunity to reflect on progress made and to define actions that will strengthen international cooperation and broaden access to benefits of space activity. Likewise, Ecuador would like to highlight its strategic vision as an equatorial state. Our privileged geographical location gives us an important position in terms of segments of geostationary orbit that positions our country as a natural, efficient, and competitive location to launch space vehicles. In this context, Ecuador invites the international community to launch its cooperation initiatives that aim at infrastructure development. in a way that allows all to take advantage of the various comparative advantages and benefit regional space development. Finally, we reiterate our commitment to the objectives of the Space 2030 Agenda, strengthening international cooperation and building outer space that is sustainable, accessible and aims to benefit all of humanity. Thank you.
Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador for the statement. And the next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Venezuela.

Good afternoon. Through its space policies, we seek to strengthen our national technological autonomy. In this context, the Ministry of Popular Power for Science and Technology, working together with the Bolivarian Agency for Space Activities, has undertaken a number of initiatives geared towards strengthening space sector institutions in Venezuela and to foster growth in this area. In this regard, my delegation is pleased to report on the first international space congress in Venezuela entitled New Challenges of Space Technology for a Shared Future, which was held in October 2025 and was attended by distinguished colleagues of the People's Republic of China, the Russian Federation, the Federative Republic of Brazil, and distinguished members of regional bodies such as the Organization of Space Cooperation for Asia Pacific, OPSO, and the Regional Center for Education in Space and Technology for Asia and the Pacific affiliated to the United Nations. We would like to highlight that this was a successful encounter based on an exchange of knowledge and addressing the challenges that we face in the area of space technology in order to build a shared future where international cooperation underpins development of countries. Chair, our delegation welcomes the convening of the first General Assembly of the Latin American and Caribbean Space Agency, ALCE, which is a landmark event. launching a new era for regional integration and cooperation in the space sector. Furthermore, we wish to congratulate Mr. Oscar Gonzalez for his designation as the Secretary General of the agency, and we trust that this represents a firm step forward guiding this agency. In 2026, we continue the scientific days that have been organized by the National Space Agency working together with the National Aquatic Space Institute, focusing on environmental preservation using space technology, including the in-field validation of data from monitoring sargassum off the Venezuelan coast, as well as an experimental study on the spectral signature of macroplastics at sea. We equally carried out research on Bird Island in order to update our digital elevation model and generated three-dimensional comprehensive modeling by merging bathymetric and geophysical data, essential in order to protect this territory and optimize geometric quality of the images of our Sucre satellite. For more than nine years now, the Sucre satellite VRSS-2 has contributed roughly one million images to our national space archive. Through this important resource, our national space agency has worked together with many national and international institutions and has promoted development in key areas such as urban planning, agriculture, health, energy, food security and the sustainable management of natural resources. As a member of the International Charter of Space and Major Disasters, the Charter, the National Space Agency has assisted countries affected by natural disasters by providing more than 10 products of added value. Regarding the mandate of this subcommittee, our delegation is of the view that there is a need to ensure ongoing coordination with the legal, the scientific and technical subcommittee in order to develop international standards to address new problematic areas, including the prohibition of any form of militarisation of outer space, the non-emplacement of any forms of weapons, the prevention of monopolies in the exploration and use of space, as well as the study of all possible modalities that will enable an equitable distribution of the benefits of space activities inter alia. Thank you, Chair. Good afternoon, dear colleagues. Once again, we'd like to draw your attention to the situation regarding the non-granting by Austrian authorities of an entry visa for this session to the head of our delegation, Special Representative and Minister of External Affairs of Russia on matters of international cooperation, the area of research and use of space for peaceful purposes, Sergei Belusko. This purely political motivation means that such decision cause damage to the professional work of this committee and the Vienna International Forum as a whole, and we urge rejection of such an approach in the name of constructive dialogue in this multilateral forum. Mr. Chair, the Russian Federation consistently expresses itself against the militarization of space and categorically rejects attempts to turn it into an arena for armed confrontation. Of particular concern are plans to develop and possibly place in space strike systems which constitutes a direct threat to global strategic stability and contradicts the spirit and letter of the Outer Space Treaty of 1967. In these conditions, it's extremely important to keep space free of any type of weapon. placing of weapons and the development of doctrines of military use of force in space could lead to unpredictable consequences all the way up to the beginning of a new armed arms race in space with the use of space resources we consider the time has come to take Collective measures to ensure transparency and strengthen trust these include conscious and voluntary rejection by each state of the use of force and the threat of force against space objects and above all unconditional rejection of placing in space arms of any kind. We believe it's counterproductive to have unilateral and purely declarative initiatives aimed at substituting real steps in the area of preventing an arms race in outer space including proposals on strengthening in the form of codes of responsible conduct in space, the commitments voluntarily undertaken by states regarding the rejection of destructive direct ascent anti-satellite missile testing. At the same time, we'd like to draw attention to the very dangerous trend of the use by a number of states of large scale constellations of small satellites and accompanying land-based infrastructure registered as civilian systems. to enable military actions of foreign armed forces and interfere in internal affairs of states. We are convinced of the unacceptability of such reckless policies which threaten common efforts of states of the global community in ensuring purely peaceful use of space technology to achieve goals of accelerated socioeconomic development for the well-being of the people of all countries. Highlighting this problem is the purpose of the renewed draft resolution of the General Assembly, Space Science and Technology for Promoting Peace. Today we had our first round of consultations on that document. We heard words of support and other proposals. The consultations on this document will continue. In addition, we've developed a short statement based on this resolution, which have been read out here on behalf of the states that are interested in doing so. This draft statement will also be available on the website of this session. Distinguished Chair, the Russian Federation shares the concerns of the global community regarding the continued process of man-made pollution of near-Earth space. And yes, we repeatedly encountered threats of collisions between the International Space Station and automatic spacecraft and space debris objects. We will continue to actively and fruitfully participate in establishing an international order to organize traffic in near earth space and the conditions of it being polluted to demand pollution under which emerging risks for space flight and the population of earth will be reduced to a safe minimum. Of key significance is oversight of space activity objects with three main components monitoring over national objects monitoring foreign and unidentified objects located in protected areas and areas of joint use of near-earth space and classification of spacecraft according to controllability criteria the Russian Federation stresses that no one state is capable of acting alone to create a global system to manage space traffic as that state wouldn't be able to obtain exhaustive information about the situation in space. In order to do this, it's necessary to have mechanism for mutually beneficial exchange of data between information and analytical national and regional centers in real time, functioning in coordination with global structures. A promising Russian system for coordination and management of space traffic will be based on the resources of the automated system to prevent dangerous situations in near-Earth space. It will ensure safe conditions for spacecraft operation and preventing collisions with other space objects during launch, when in orbit, and during withdrawal from orbit after service. This will allow for the management of a large number of spacecraft from megaconstellations. In future, we plan to create an open information platform to exchange information about space objects and dangerous events in near-Earth space, as well as planned launches of spacecraft and orbit maneuvers, as well as joint analysis of complex in-flight or emergency situations and accompaniment of uncontrolled descent from orbit of large spacecraft. The Russian Federation aims to participate in constructive dialogue on the full specter of issues on the international space agenda with a focus on maintaining space for peaceful purposes. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you. I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. Please generally keep in mind the time limit for the intervention. And the next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Australia.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished delegates. Over the past two decades, space-based technologies have become indispensable to modern life and global economic prosperity, providing critical services to address global challenges. At the same time, the space environment is becoming increasingly crowded and contested. All States must work collectively to establish effective measures to ensure the safety, security and sustainability of outer space. In a period of geopolitical tension, continued cooperation through existing multilateral frameworks is essential to ensure space remains peaceful and accessible to all. Chair, we recognize the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space as a central United Nations platform for issues related to the peaceful use of outer space. Its work forms part of a broad international framework complemented by UN disarmament bodies, particularly the General Assembly's First Committee, which plays a vital role in advancing initiatives that encourage responsible behaviour, reduce tensions and prevent miscalculation. Australia supports discussions in the open-ended working group on the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. Australia strongly advocates for a behaviour-based, non-binding space security framework, which offers flexibility in response to rapidly evolving dual-use technologies while fostering trust and mutual understanding among space actors. The guidelines for the long-term sustainability of outer space activities could serve as a model for such a framework. Chair, it is important that these discussions continue to strengthen dialogue and cooperation on space security. Australia continues to work with regional partners to this end. In November 2025, Australia co-chaired the ASEAN Regional Forum workshop on peace and security in outer space with Philippines and Singapore. The workshop brought together ARF participants and international experts to deepen regional understanding, contextualize global discussions within the Indo-Pacific and build capacity on practical measures for peaceful and sustainable space use. Discussions emphasized the importance of a pragmatic, incremental approach grounded in cooperation, transparency and confidence building. The workshop also underscored the need for stronger links across multilateral system. Geneva-based disarmament discussions and Vienna-based work on space safety and sustainability should be complementary and not pursued in silos. In this regard, COPUOS, supported by the UN Office of Outer Space Affairs, plays a critical role in advancing cooperation, information sharing and best practices. Joint sessions of the UNGA First and Fourth Committees focused on outer space have played a useful role in building links and breaking down silos, and we welcome future such sessions. Australia welcomes continued dialogue on these issues and looks forward to the active participation in the upcoming meetings of the UN open-ended Working Group. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia for the statement. And the next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Japan.

Japan's government will support these efforts in collaboration with UNOSA. And Chair, Japan will remain committed to upholding the rule of law in outer space, advancing space debris mitigation and remediation, promoting the effective implementation of LTS guidelines, and for practical international cooperation. Japan is ready to work with all member countries to ensure the peaceful and sustainable use of outer space for benefits of all. Thank you so much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan for the statement. And the next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Mr. President.

Mr. Chair. Columbia reiterates its concern regarding recent actions that depart from the spirit of cooperation and multilateralism focused on peaceful and consensus-based resolution of conflicts. Therefore, we call for maintaining the spirit of cooperation and multilateralism to support the well-being and coexistence of all human beings, and to maintain our focus on seeking progress and resolving the needs and challenges humanity is affected by. It is imperative that all efforts be made to ensure that outer space not be used to deploy any type of weapon in space. In the same way, it's important to mention that orbital space that is congested, unsafe, or inaccessible undermines the ability of all states to benefit from space activities, disproportionately affecting countries with emerging space capacities. In this regard, Colombia recalls that the Outer Space Treaty states that exploration and use of outer space must be done exclusively for peaceful purposes and to benefit all of humanity. In addition, Colombia considers that constant monitoring of orbital space, including trajectories, potential collisions, and anomalous behavior of space objects allow for mitigating risks and preventing incidents that could lead to tensions between states. Therefore, we recognize that space situational awareness is a critical capacity to ensure operational security of space activities. In this regard, Columbia appreciates multilateral efforts to build integrated and open orbital initiatives and we consider it fundamental that countries both with advanced capacities and countries with emerging capacities participate actively in this global exercise of collaborative space oversight. Colombia encourages all states to strengthen transparency in their space activities including timely notification on launches, sharing of information on missions, and registry of space objects in accordance with the Convention on Registration. Likewise, we highlight the progress made in the different working groups of the subcommittees, in the Action Team on Lunar Activities Consultations, ATLAC, and the other mechanisms that focus on coordinating and cooperating to resolve current problems and ensure long-term sustainability of space activity. Now that we have a closer view of exploration, exploitation and use of outer space, we need the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, UNOSA, to also be strengthened, and the role of this committee must respond effectively to the new challenges that we face. Thus, the results of UNISPACE-4 should also focus on objectives that will provide sustainable, fair and equitable solutions. It is only through global governance that is based on trust, technical cooperation and respect will it be possible to ensure that outer space continues to be a place for peace, development and cooperation between nations. Thank you.

Thank you. Good afternoon, distinguished delegates. My name is Mashallah Shememry. I'm the managing director for the Center for Space Futures. The center is a global platform established by the Saudi Space Agency in collaboration with the World Economic Forum to help advance the future of the space economy through policy, technology, insights, and cross-sector collaboration. Today, I will share findings from our joint report, Clear Orbit, Secure Future, which examines the economic impact of space debris. The purpose of this presentation is not only to share the findings, but also to invite member states to engage with us, test the recommendations, and help move this work forward toward practical implementation. Space infrastructure has become essential to modern life on Earth. It supports communication, navigation, earth observation, disaster response, finance, agriculture, and security. But the orbital environment that enables these services is becoming more congested, more fragile, and more costly to operate in. Space debris is no longer only a technical issue. It is now an economic, operational, and governance challenge. That is why this topic matters not only to satellite operators, but also to member states responsible for policy, licensing, safety, and long-term sustainability. Member states should care because space systems are now critical infrastructure. When satellite services are disrupted, the consequences can extend beyond the space sector and affect economies, public services, emergency response, and national capabilities. At the same time, orbital congestion and debris accumulation are intensifying in key low Earth orbit bands. This study was developed to provide a common evidence base. First, the physical modeling projects how the debris environment evolves from 2025 to 2040 under business as usual. Then the analysis translates the environment into operational risk and finally into economic losses from anomalies, failures and avoidance maneuvers between 2025 and 2035. To understand the economic impact, we first need we first needed to understand how the debris environment evolves. The model shows. The debris risk is not spread evenly across low Earth orbit. It is concentrated in specific altitude bands, particularly around 775, 840, and 1,000 kilometers, where derelict objects and fragment clouds overlap. This matters because these are not just empty numbers on a chart. They represent orbital regions where the density and persistence of debris creates higher collision risk for current and future missions. The challenge is especially serious because much of the operational risk comes from smaller non trackable fragments. These fragments may be too small to reliably monitor, but they can still degrade spacecraft performance or even end emission above approximately 700 kilometers. It is important to note the debris can remain in orbit for centuries. This means today's behavior. can create a long-term operating constraints for future generations of space activities. Once the model identifies where debris risk is concentrated, the next step is to understand how that risk becomes economic cost. The study focuses on three main pathways. These are anomalies from small debris, mission-ending impacts, and collision avoidance maneuvers. The first pathway is anomalies caused by small non-trackable debris. These events may not destroy a satellite, but they can interrupt service, degrade performance, and require diagnostic and recovery efforts. Because these incidents can occur repeatedly across many satellites, they become the largest cost driver in the analysis. The second pathway is mission-ending impact, where debris causes total satellite loss. That creates replacement cost, launch costs, service losses and potential insurance exposure. The third pathway is the growing burden of avoidance maneuvers, which consumes fuel, shortens lifetime and increases operational complexity. When these risks are translated into economic terms, the result is clear. Under business as usual, debris could impose between 25.8 and 42.3 billion US dollars in projected losses between 2025 and 2035. Notably, this estimate does not assume a major catastrophic event or cascading collision scenario. I want to emphasize that this is a business as usual case. The largest share of the cost comes from anomalies caused by small debris estimated at 14.2 to $30.7 billion. Mission ending impacts, which adds approximately $11.1 billion, while avoidance maneuvers add around $560 million. The maneuver figure is smaller, but it still reflects a growing operational burden that accumulates over time. The main point is that the economic burden is not driven only by dramatic collision. It is also driven by repeated disruptions, degraded performance, and operational costs that compound across constellations and years of service. In that sense, debris becomes a persistent economic drag on the space economy. The projected losses are not inevitable. Targeted action today can help prevent exponential costs tomorrow, but the action needs to be coordinated across multiple areas. The report highlights four practical areas where progress is needed. First, we need stronger monitoring and data sharing. This includes expanding tracking coverage in high risk orbital zones, improving data accuracy and strengthening interoperability between systems. Better information is the foundation for better risk management. Second, mitigation standards need to be strengthened and implemented more consistently. This includes end of life disposal, passivation, design for demise considerations and verification mechanisms. Third, active debris removal needs to move from demonstration towards scalable and cost effective approaches, especially for large debris in critical orbits. Finally, global governance remains essential. No single actor can solve this challenge alone, and no single national system can fully manage a shared orbital environment. More coherent norms, transparency, responsibility, coordination, and shared implementation lessons will be central to reducing the cost of inaction. This is where we would like to invite member states to engage with us. First, as you can see from the presentation, there's a QR code you can scan right now with your phones. We invite you to read the paper that we published and review the assumptions, methodologies, findings, and recommendations. We want the analysis to be useful, but we also want it to be tested and challenged by those working on implementation. Second, we invite Member States to assess how the recommendation applies to national context. This includes licensing systems, regulatory frameworks, operational realities, and implementation capacities. Different countries will face different challenges, and that feedback is important for making the recommendations more practical. Third, we welcome feedback on what is feasible, what is missing, and where further work is needed. Our goal is not to prescribe a single model. It is to help move from shared principles towards practical, testable implementation that can support a safer and more sustainable orbital environment. With that, I encourage you to engage with us by scanning this QR code, which gives you our contact to share your ideas and feedback. So finally, I will close by encouraging you to access the full report, engage with us using this QR code, which allows you to reach out directly to the Center for Space Futures to provide your feedback. We are especially interested in your views on implementation barriers, data gaps, and how these recommendations could best could be tested in different national or regional contexts. The cost of inaction is measurable. The risk is shared and the response must be coordinated. Thank you and we look forward to continuing the conversation with you.

Good afternoon, Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates, members of the committee. My name is Carsten Schallmann, I represent a young Austrian space company, our space. In such an environment, companies face intense competition and increasingly aggressive timelines. As a result, they accept higher levels of risk. In aerospace, we often say that failure is not an option. However, in such an environment, failures continue to occur, particularly when systems are deployed without sufficient validation. This problem is directly linked to sustainability. We call it infant mortalities when satellites fail early and prematurely. When they do, they may become inactive, incorporative objects in orbit and contribute to the growing space debris problem. For that reason, in-orbit demonstrations, or IOD, is becoming an increasingly important element in our space economy. Validating technologies under actual space conditions and on a reliable space proven satellite platform reduces risk and ultimately contributes to a more sustainable space environment. However, despite its importance of IODs, access to in-orbit demonstrations remain difficult. Current solutions are often expensive, technically complex and associated with long lead items. For many startups and innovative technology developers, those barriers delay or even kill their commercialization efforts, causing bankruptcy and therefore slowing globally the advance of space technology and of our global space economy. To address this challenge, our space has developed the so-called Green Box Service, an innovative in-orbit demonstration service designed specifically to reduce the barrier of flight testing.

How can I go back?

Our objective is straightforward. We want to make in-orbit demonstrations faster, simpler, and more affordable. Our experiences in the last years have shown and compared with traditional approaches, our Green Box service reduces the lead time 50% and more, reduces the cost 60% and brings down the overall complexity for participating companies around 80%. So how are we doing this? The GreenBox service is built around three key elements. Firstly, we developed a dedicated satellite platform designed specifically for in-orbit validation missions. Secondly, a standardized patented payload accommodation unit, a container, which protects the payload and simplifies the integration. Thirdly, our space provides a holistic service model including the satellite qualification testing, launch and operation in space. The market response up to now from our customers has been extremely encouraging and we are launching our first satellite with three customers later this year and our second satellite is already in preparation. We are very proud that this first Austrian commercial satellite was entirely developed and built in Austria and will be launched by European launch provider ESA Aerospace, built in Austria, launched by Europe. Some quick words about two of our customers, Sunbooster, it's an Austrian company specializing in photovoltaic technologies. They developed a much cheaper type of photovoltaic cells, potentially bringing down the cost of power in space, a factor of two or three hundred, which is a very important point when you have, for example, space-based data centers or other power hungry infrastructure in space on your mind. Second example is Synopsys Planet from Portugal who will be also on our first flight. The company has developed a system that can function both as a star tracker for spacecraft navigation as well as a tool for space debris detection. In particular, the latter is of ultimate importance in a congested orbit and for sustainable space. Synopsys Planet was selected and integrated into our satellite in a record low time of only five months, proving my earlier statements referring to the efficiency of the Green Box satellite service. In conclusion, the further growth of the space economy depends not only on our innovative potential and engineering capabilities, but also on the reliability and sustainability of our efforts. As more and more actors enter space, we must ensure that new technologies are probably validated before widespread deployment. Our space is supporting this so that space is usable for all of us and for a long time to come. With this, I'd like to conclude and thank you very much for your attention.

Good day, distinguished delegates. The Philippine Space Agency is pleased to share updates on space science and technology applications for sustainable development. These activities reflect the Philippine Space Agency's continuing efforts to operationalize space science and technology in support of agriculture, disaster risk resilience, climate action, and capacity building. particularly in line with national development priorities and the sustainable development goals. As an archipelagic country situated in the Western Pacific, the Philippines faces unique development challenges. The country consistently ranks high in global disaster risk indices, creating significant demands for connectivity, environmental monitoring, and disaster preparedness across thousands of islands. Relying solely on traditional ground-based systems presents challenges in ensuring that national and local efforts are efficient, effective, and timely. With an average of 20 typhoons annually and frequent tectonic activity, continuous monitoring and early warning are critical for disaster preparedness and response. As climate change poses increasing risks to development in the country, space technologies have become critical tools for advancing sustainable development, strengthening resilience, and supporting inclusive growth for Filipinos. The establishment of the Philippine Space Agency in 2019 marked a significant milestone in the country's efforts to harness space for sustainable development. With the vision of bringing the benefits of space closer to the lives of Filipinos, PhilSA has pursued programs and initiatives that leverage space science technology and applications to address national priorities. Through the Space for SDGs approach, the agency contributes to advancing the sustainable development goals while fostering resilience, innovation, and inclusive growth. PHILSA's initiatives demonstrate how investments in space capabilities can generate tangible benefits across multiple sectors. Starting with developing our own upstream capabilities, PHILSA commits to building indigenous space capabilities through the MAYA, DIWATA, and MULA satellite development. These missions strengthen national capacity in satellite engineering, Earth observation, and scientific research while generating valuable data for environmental monitoring and resource management. Beyond the satellites themselves, these programs contribute to the development of a highly skilled workforce that will sustain the country's long-term space endeavors. Through the PhilSat Integrated Network of Space Enabled Options Towards Sustainability or the PINAST project, satellite data, geospatial information, and space-based applications are made more accessible to government agencies, researchers, academic institutions, and local stakeholders. The project serves as a venue for translating Earth observation data into actionable information products that support evidence-based decision-making across sectors. By promoting data sharing, capacity building, and the wider use of space technology, the PINAS project helps strengthen disaster risk reduction and management, environmental monitoring, natural resource management, and local development planning. contributing to a more sustainable and resilient communities. Space data has also been increasingly utilized to support environmental monitoring, ecosystem conservation, and disaster risk reduction and management. Through satellite-based mapping and assessment activities, FILSA contributes to the monitoring of mangroves, seagrass beds, coral reef ecosystems, coastal habitats, and other environmentally significant areas. More recently, FLSA has supported disaster and environmental monitoring efforts through the generation of ashfall extent maps following volcanic events, satellite-based flood mapping for rapid impact assessment, and the use of earth observation data to monitor air quality conditions. These information products provide timely and actionable insights for government agencies and local communities, supporting environmental protection, disaster preparedness response, and recovery efforts. International cooperation remains a cornerstone of our work. Through bilateral and multilateral initiatives, including Copernicus Philippines program and its SCOPE Digital project, FILSA continues to strengthen knowledge exchange, technical capacity, and access to space-based solutions for sustainable development. Spoke Digital supports the development of digital innovation and earth observation applications by expanding access to Copernicus data, not just in the country, but also in Southeast Asia, fostering local expertise and enabling the use of satellite information for evidence-based decision-making across government, academia, and industry. Together with partnerships with regional and international space agencies, these efforts help advance the use of space technologies to address national development priorities and contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Collectively, these initiatives demonstrate how space-derived information can support better decisions across agriculture, disaster management, environmental protection, and national development. As an agricultural country, the Philippines benefits from space technologies that support food security and climate resilience. To advance these efforts, PhilSat develops and operationalizes satellite-derived data products for the agriculture sector. One example is the Drought Early Warning in the Philippines or the D2PH project, which generates agricultural drought forecast maps using satellite-derived rainfall, temperature, and vegetation data. The system integrates multiple earth observation datasets to monitor drought development. Rainfall products assess precipitation deficits, land surface temperature data capture heat stress, and vegetation indices monitor crop and vegetation health. These datasets are processed into indicators that characterize drought conditions across the country. Using historical satellite observations and statistical and machine learning techniques, the system identifies relationships among rainfall variability, temperature anomalies, vegetation response, and drought progression. It then forecasts the likelihood and severity of drought several months ahead, producing maps that identify areas at risk of soil moisture deficits, vegetation stress, and reduced agricultural productivity. These products provide timely information that supports proactive planning, resource allocation, and preparedness measures, helping government agencies and agricultural stakeholders mitigate the impacts of climate-related hazards. How do these efforts translate into concrete action? One example is PhilSA's ongoing support for preparations for the anticipated impacts of El Nino. The Philippines Department of Agriculture, together with the Philippine Weather Bureau and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, has been coordinating with regional offices nationwide to strengthen preparedness. In these efforts, PhilSat agricultural drought products serve as an important decision support tool. By providing timely information on the progression of drought conditions, affected areas, and the potential severity of impacts on crops, the information supports the prioritization of interventions in areas expected to experience severe drought stress. This includes informing the timing and targeting of cloud seeding operations, supporting irrigation management, and helping identify communities and stakeholders that may require targeted livelihood support and aid. Through these applications, satellite-derived drought forecasting moves beyond monitoring and becomes a practical tool for anticipatory action, enabling stakeholders to prepare for drought conditions before impacts become severe, thereby strengthening food security efforts across the country. In summary, Our experience demonstrates that investments in space are ultimately investments in sustainable development. Through Earth observation, innovation, capacity building, and international cooperation, space technologies are delivering tangible benefits to communities while supporting national efforts toward resilience, sustainability, and inclusive growth. As an emerging space actor, the Philippine Space Agency reaffirms its commitment to harnessing space science, technology, and applications for the benefit of all Filipinos. The Philippines looks forward to strengthening collaboration in advancing the use of space for the achievement of the sustainable development goals. Thank you.
